conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martínez, the perinatal-mental-health clinician here. I’m so glad you came in today—how are you feeling?

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you to do something we call the EPDS (it stands for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s a short, well-trusted set of 10 questions that helps us understand how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers; this is simply a way for us to make sure we’re catching anything that might be making these early weeks harder than they need to be.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team directly involved in your care. My goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space so you can speak openly. After each question I’ll just jot down a quick note—no lengthy forms on your side.

We’ll go through ten questions, one at a time, about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. Ready to start?

Here’s the first question:
In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Oh… yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh. I mean, it’s not like before the baby, when everything felt light or spontaneous, but if my partner makes a joke or I see something silly online, I’ll still chuckle. It doesn’t feel forced or anything—just maybe a little less often because I’m tired.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that sounds right—I still laugh and find things funny, just maybe not as easily as before.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do still look forward to stuff—like my sister’s coming over tomorrow with coffee, and I’m excited about that. It’s not every single thing, but little outings or even just a quiet shower feel nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I might think, “Did I eat something that bothered him?”—but it’s fleeting. I don’t sit there beating myself up. I figure babies are just unpredictable and I’m learning.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get little flashes of worry—like I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds normal or if I’m burping him right—but it passes quickly once I check on him. It’s not constant, and I can usually talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any panicky moments—no racing heart or sense of doom. Just those quick “is he okay?” thoughts, then I’m fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m keeping up. Sure, there are stretches—like yesterday when he wouldn’t nap and laundry piled up—but I still managed to get the bottles washed and throw together tacos for dinner. I wouldn’t say I’m drowning; it’s just a bit hectic sometimes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, my mood hasn’t messed with my sleep. I crash pretty hard once the baby’s down for the night. I might wake up when he cries to feed, but I fall right back asleep. I haven’t lain there feeling unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t call it sad—more like tired and a little stretched. I still smile at the baby’s funny faces and enjoy when my older niece sends me silly videos. I haven’t had that heavy, gloomy feeling.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much at all. Maybe once when I was super tired and the baby wouldn’t latch, but it was just a couple tears and I was over it in minutes. It’s definitely not a daily thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [enter today]  
Source: Self-report on 10-item EPDS analogue  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Mild reduction in ability to laugh/find humor (“not as easily as before”)  
- Fleeting, situational worries about infant care (breathing, burping, latch); resolves quickly without panic  
- Occasional “flashes” of self-blame limited to infant spit-up or sleep issues; no pervasive guilt  

<sym>Symptoms denied</sym>  
- Persistent sadness, tearfulness, or crying spells  
- Loss of interest/pleasure in most activities (reports looking forward to sister’s visit, quiet shower)  
- Mood-related insomnia (sleep disrupted only by infant needs)  
- Panic episodes, sense of doom, or physiological panic  
- Self-harm or suicidal ideation  

Pattern/Clinical Impression  
No consistent evidence of major depressive or anxiety symptoms above subclinical threshold. Stressors appear normative for early postpartum period (fatigue, role adjustment). Denies safety concerns.

Risk Level: Low for postpartum depression or anxiety disorder at this time; routine paediatric/primary-care follow-up recommended. Re-screen if worsening mood, functioning, or new safety issues arise.
